extracted.intended_audience: general educated readers of philosophical, political, and literary essays (19th-century)
extracted.subtask_short: philosophical essays on politics and aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of prescriptive and evaluative maxims for political conduct, religious understanding, aesthetics (beauty, epic poetry, colour theory), rhetorical method, and historical judgment as given in short philosophical essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of metaphysical studies
rubrics_metrics.description: No studies give such a power of distinguishing as metaphysical, and in their natural and unperverted tendency they are ennobling and exalting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphysical study trains the power of distinguishing and ennobles the mind; it counteracts the narrowing effects of legal studies and practice. Use metaphysical reflection to develop subtle judgement rather than merely instrumental skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for legitimate constitutional change
rubrics_metrics.description: If the nation demands the abolition of the hereditary peerage, the king and the deputies should form a constituent assembly to act in the name of the total nation and decree abolition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fundamental constitutional changes should be enacted by a body legitimately representing the whole nation (a constituent assembly) rather than by a subordinate chamber yielding under pressure; peers may withdraw to private life but should not be coerced into betraying their office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mobilising passions to preclude deliberation
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments must not carry fundamental changes by exciting the passions and playing upon the necessary ignorance of the numerical majority so that free and competent discussion is precluded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should avoid appealing solely to mass sentiment or numerical majorities (regardless of competence or sobriety) when making fundamental governmental changes; preserve forums for informed, calm deliberation and representation of interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religion must combine ideas and facts
rubrics_metrics.description: A true religion must consist of ideas and facts both; not of ideas alone (mere Philosophy), nor of facts alone (mere History).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious systems or narratives intended to be 'true' should anchor doctrinal ideas in historical facts and use facts as symbols grounded in ideas; neither pure abstract speculation nor mere historical chronicle suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: State as intermediate whole, not mere aggregate
rubrics_metrics.description: A State is an idea intermediate between the inorganic (a mere collection) and the organic (where the whole subsumes the parts): 'the whole being a result from, and not a mere total of, the parts, and yet not so merging the constituent parts in the result, but that the individual exists integrally within it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing political communities, treat the State as an integrated idea in which individuals retain integral existence rather than as either a simple sum of parts or as totalitarian fusion; avoid theories that either annihilate individual worth or treat persons only as things.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persons versus things (ethical-political criterion)
rubrics_metrics.description: All social law and justice are grounded on the principle that a person can never, but by his own fault, become a thing, or be treated as such; a thing may be used altogether as a means, but the person must always be included in the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and law should treat human beings as ends in themselves; institutions that reduce persons to mere means violate the moral code of a civilized society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty = multitude in unity
rubrics_metrics.description: The old definition of beauty in the Roman school of painting was 'il più nell' uno' — multitude in unity; superior minds instinctively endeavour to bring into unity the scattered facts which occur in conversation or statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In art and composition, seek to unify diverse elements into a coherent whole; strong creative work gathers scattered details into a single organizing idea or form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity-seeking as a mark of genius
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most characteristic and infallible criteria of the different ranks of men's intellects is the instinctive habit of superior minds to endeavour to bring, and never rest till they have brought, into unity the scattered facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate creative intelligence by its tendency to synthesize and unify material; in producing work, cultivate the habit of unifying disparate details into an overarching conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facts are not sufficient for argument; require legitimate deduction
rubrics_metrics.description: To attempt to argue any great question upon facts only is absurd; facts are not truths, not conclusions, not even premisses, but parts of premisses. The truth depends on, and is only arrived at, by a legitimate deduction from all the facts which are truly material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In rhetoric and reasoning (including persuasive writing), do not rely solely on isolated facts; assemble all genuinely material facts and apply proper reasoning/deduction to reach conclusions. Beware of selective fact-use and of treating facts as self-evident truths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church discipline necessary even in pure democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Even to a church — the only pure democracy, because in it persons are alone considered and one person à priori is equal to another — discipline is an essential condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Communal or institutional forms that treat persons equally still require rules and discipline to function; in organizing groups (including literary or artistic communities), maintain structures that preserve order and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess motives, not merely professions (religious critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Dissenters profess zeal for Christianity, but in many cases their hatred to the Church of England is a much more active principle of action than their love for Christianity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating movements or actors, look beyond stated beliefs to underlying motives; critique that focuses only on outward profession risks misunderstanding driving forces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Franchise extension — avoid nominal extension causing practical disfranchisement
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere extension of the franchise is not the evil; the mischief is that the franchise is nominally extended, but to such classes, and in such a manner, that a practical disfranchisement of all above, and a discontenting of all below, a favoured class are the unavoidable results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In reforms, design changes so they do not create new imbalances or privileged classes; extend rights in ways that preserve meaningful representation for existing constituencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epic subject selection and method
rubrics_metrics.description: The destruction of Jerusalem is the only subject now remaining for an epic poem; there must be a mythology, or a quasi-mythology, for an epic poem; difficulties must be mitigated and thrown into the shade as Milton did.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For epic composition, choose a subject of universal resonance and provide (or invent) a suitable mythic framework; anticipate and strategically soften historical or factual difficulties to serve a grand poetic design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colour representation via heptad (formal device)
rubrics_metrics.description: Colours may best be expressed by a heptad, the largest possible formula for things finite, as the pentad is the smallest possible form. The heptad of things finite is reducible to the pentad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When organizing a colour scheme or symbolic colour system in creative work, consider a structured multi-part taxonomy (here, sevenfold) to capture relations (prothesis, thesis, antithesis, synthesis, etc.); use such a system to give colours formal and symbolic coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmony founded on relation to rest; role of clerisy
rubrics_metrics.description: All harmony is founded on a relation to rest — on relative rest. The clerisy of a nation, its learned men, whether poets or philosophers or scholars, are these points of relative rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cultural or aesthetic composition, seek points of stability around which harmonic relations form; recognize and cultivate 'stable' canonical voices or institutions that sustain cultural order and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotyped common phrases; value craft over facile style
rubrics_metrics.description: Common phrases are so stereotyped by conventional use that it is much easier to write ordinary politics in the common newspaper style than it is to make a good pair of shoes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cliché and facile, conventional phraseology in writing; value craftsmanship and the harder work of producing fresh, carefully constructed prose or verse rather than resorting to ready-made journalistic formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate historical thinkers in their context (counterfactual empathy)
rubrics_metrics.description: To estimate a man like Vico, or any great man who has made discoveries and committed errors, you ought to say to yourself — 'He did so and so in the year 1720, a Papist, at Naples. Now, what would he not have done if he had lived now, and could have availed himself of all our vast acquisitions in physical science?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When critiquing past authors, account for their historical circumstances and imagine how their thought might have developed with later knowledge; avoid anachronistic condemnation by contextualizing achievements and errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Canon formation criterion: catholicity over mere genuineness
rubrics_metrics.description: The ancient Church was not guided by the mere fact of the genuineness of a writing in pronouncing it canonical — its catholicity was the test applied to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When determining the value or authority of texts (religious or literary), consider their reception, usefulness, and acceptance (catholicity) within the community over strictly provenance-based authenticity alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dictation vs. inspiration in authorship and reading
rubrics_metrics.description: There may be dictation without inspiration, and inspiration without dictation; revelation and inspiration were manifested but not necessarily literal dictation, and one should read the Bible as a book with human intellectual shaping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret authoritative texts (sacred or canonical literature) with allowance for human faculty and individuality in composition; do not demand literal verbal dictation to accept spiritual truth — read attentively and use scholarly means to apprehend general sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epidemic causation triad and practical responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Three factors of the operation of an epidemic or atmospheric disease: (1) the predisposed state of the body; (2) the specific virus in the atmosphere; (3) accidental circumstances of weather, locality, food, occupation. Against the second we are powerless; medicine may act profitably against the first; a wise medical police ought to be adopted against the third. Quarantine cannot keep out an atmospheric disease; but it can, and does always, increase the predisposing causes of its reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public-health policy and medical responses should target predisposing conditions and environmental/administrative factors; understand limits of quarantine and focus on strengthening bodies and improving local conditions rather than relying solely on exclusionary measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral law of polarity (cycles of extremes)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the maximum of one tendency has been attained, there is no gradual decrease but a direct transition to its minimum till the opposite tendency attains its maximum; e.g., Restoration led to mechanico-corpuscular philosophy and later revolution to subjectivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyzing political and cultural trends (or structuring dramatic arcs), anticipate oscillations between extremes; avoid assuming gradual moderation — periods of excess may be followed by swift reversals.
